description:
White Rock lake, lower spillway
4 part series of a mock snowy battle.
Texas Death Match Snowy Style 
1.  A snowy egret (just out of sight here)  was busy catching fish when this second snowy walked up behind it & sprang into the air to challenge for this prime fishing spot.   You can see the path of drops where it's feet had just left the water.
2.  The first egret accepted the challenge and it was on.  Both birds were in mid air going at it.  They were not flying, they would jump in the  air with loud squawks and try to intimidate with spread wings and head feathers puffed up.
3.  Both fell back down to the ground & the one on the right chased the original one to the left, away from the prime fishing spot.  Looks like it was using its tongue also to intimidate. 
4.  With the first bird gone, the interloper took a victory walk for a few seconds as though to say "That's right!  I'm bad!"    The entire encounter took less than a minute according to the time stamps on my photos.

description:
White Rock lake
Pool by Winsted parking lot
Photo 1:
Almost Like a Ballet
First thing I do  at the spillway is to look over the fence to see if any wildlife is by the parking lot.  This time I had to scramble to get my camera up to capture a battle in progress.  Snowy egrets are known for engaging in mock territorial battles.  They look fierce but they never actually come in contact or inflict injuries.  I didn't have time to focus or fiddle, all I could do was point & click as quick as possible.
Photo 2:
This Battle Is Not Mock
They both leaped in the air so suddenly I didn't get all of the top one in this shot.  But it dawned on me that this was not the usual mock battle.  Contact was definitely being made.
Photo 3:
The Iron Claw
This reminded me of a wrestling move as the top snowy drove a sharp toenail into the skull of the lower sno
Photo 4:
Death Grip
Check out the grip they have on each other's foot!  And the one on top is driving that beak into the head of the lower one.  For sure not a mock battle.  This was the last shot I got.  The next action happened too fast for me to keep up.  Lower bird broke the grip and flew over the tree line with the other in hot pursuit.

Snowy Egret (Egretta thula) is a small and graceful egret in the Small Egrets and Herons (Egretta) genus and the Typical Herons and Egrets (Ardeinae) subfamily that is 24 inches long with 41 inch wingspan. Adult has a black bill, black legs, and yellow feet. Legs of immatures and non-breeding adults have greenish-yellow up back of leg. Snowy Egret is widespead in coastal wetlands and other marine and freshwater habitats. It alternates active wading, foot-stirring, and even dashing around erratically to stir up prey.
Snowy Egret is known for its yellow feet and is said "to dance in the shallows on golden slippers." It has white lacy plumes on head, breast, and back during breeding season. Egrets suffered huge population collapses at the end of the 19th century from the harvesting of these delicate plumes for ladies hats. Lores (skin between eye and bill) are usually bright yellow, but flush reddish in the breeding season. Juveniles have duller yellow lores and more yellow extending up the legs than adults. Snowy Egret is fairly common and widespread in North and South America and is most common along the coast. It forages actively in shallow water, often darting after small fish. It is widespread in many types of aquatic habitats, including fresh and salt water. It nests in colonies in trees, shrubs, mangroves, sometimes on or near the ground in protected marshes. Diet is varied and includes fish, crabs, crayfish, frogs, snakes, insects, snails, worms, lizards, and even small rodents."
